title: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android
gist: Ars reviews Google's new Android-based Googlebook laptops, finding solid premium OEM hardware but a phone-first OS with few desktop-grade apps, buggy phone integration and underwhelming AI features at $899-$1,300+. The reviewer questions whether Googlebooks need to exist alongside Chromebooks and doubts Google's persistence.

insights.claim: Googlebooks skip the budget segment that made Chromebooks successful, with most of the lineup well over $1,000: Acer Googlebook 14 at $899 (limited-time), Dell XPS at $999, Lenovo from $1,100 and Snapdragon X Elite HP Googlebook 14 at $1,300.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Google is targeting premium laptops, competing directly with Windows and MacBook Air price points.

insights.claim: At $1,300, the entry-level MacBook Air is probably a better overall option for most people, because premium Googlebooks face the same problem as premium Windows laptops.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Price-value gap versus Apple limits Googlebook share capture.
insights.locator: I appreciate that Google is pushing

insights.claim: Launch Googlebooks come in Intel and Snapdragon variants that perform similarly overall, though Snapdragon appears to have a higher performance ceiling and better gaming, and some reports cite app issues on Intel models.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Silicon choice is a minor differentiator; software is the bottleneck.
insights.locator: Googlebooks come in both Intel and Snapdragon variants

insights.claim: Googlebook OS is still Android under the hood, and the reviewer says it almost never feels like a premium laptop, with apps closing in the background due to memory-constrained design and needing to reload.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Core platform design mismatch is the central risk to the Googlebook thesis.
insights.quote: It almost never feels like using a premium laptop, and that’s the problem.

insights.claim: Phone integration needs Android 17, which most phones lack, and features such as Continue On, notification sync, file access and app mirroring are buggy, limited to one app at a time and one-way for file access.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Android 17 update penetration gates the ecosystem benefit; watch rollout.
insights.locator: Setting up a Googlebook is a snap

insights.claim: Google's desktop software lags: the Files app lacks tabs and network shares, and split-screen and multiple desktops work but are less intuitive and capable than macOS or Windows.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Basic desktop gaps are what drive power users away.

insights.claim: Drive, Gmail and Calendar are progressive web apps on Googlebooks, and Dropbox is unoptimized, so cloud-sync functionality is weaker than on Windows or macOS and offers no advantage over a much cheaper Chromebook.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Google's own apps not native to its platform undermine the pitch.
insights.quote: If you’re just going to end up in a web app, why not buy a Chromebook for a third of the price?
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the Drive app isn’t even an Android app

insights.claim: Developers only build for what people use and no one has demanded desktop-style Android apps, leaving Google in a chicken-and-egg bind where most Play Store apps are tagged only 'Compatible with desktop' or 'Built for mobile'.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Weak app optimization incentives mean the ecosystem gap may persist for years.
insights.quote: Developers only build for what people use

insights.claim: Even optimized apps disappoint: Adobe Photoshop on Googlebooks has a poorly scaled mobile UI with few keyboard shortcuts, and Slack is abysmal outside a phone and cannot be installed as a PWA currently.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Major software vendors have not committed real desktop effort to Android laptops.
insights.locator: Even apps that have been optimized for desktop

insights.claim: Magic Pointer, which hands screen content to Gemini via cursor wiggle, is hardly revolutionary and Gemini inaccuracy means even calendar appointments can fail, requiring the user to double-check almost everything; Create My Widget is mostly useless due to limited content access.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Tentpole AI features underdeliver, weakening the differentiation versus Windows Copilot and macOS.
insights.locator: AI is a big part of the Googlebook experience

insights.claim: Rambler, an AI voice input feature debuted on Pixel 11 and included on all Googlebooks, works in any text field and is likely to impress most users.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: One AI feature with genuine utility.
insights.locator: Rambler, which debuted on the Pixel 11 lineup

insights.claim: Antigravity, Google's AI-centric dev app included on every Googlebook, built a functional but buggy file manager with the default Gemini Flash model in minutes, but making it reliable took hours of prompting over days and required paying for AI compute.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Vibe coding can patch app gaps but is not a substitute for a finished platform; it also drives AI compute demand.
insights.locator: After struggling with the Files app for a few days

insights.claim: Apps built with Antigravity are treated as special sideloads, scanned by Play Protect without enabling unknown sources, and Google confirms they won't be affected by developer verification when it rolls out on Googlebooks next year.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Google is carving out a path for AI-generated apps within its sideloading restrictions.

insights.claim: The reviewer asks whether Googlebooks need to exist given established Chromebooks, concludes they are not a viable alternative to macOS and Windows yet, and is skeptical Google will persist given its recent history.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Execution and commitment risk is the main concern; treat as a multi-year, uncertain effort.
insights.quote: Does Google have the patience to spend years doing this work?
insights.locator: The first step on a long road
